body_text: For the rare gaming enthusiast who’s somehow in two minds about whether to bother with undoubtedly the most hyped videogame of all time, GTA VI, a new offer from telecoms giant Virgin Media might just tip the scales. According to a new post on the TV and WiFi provider’s Irish website, Virgin will give one lucky winner €100 (~$111) an hour to play the game when it drops on November 19, handing over almost $900 for a full eight-hour shift as well as a free copy of the game. The gamer can clock up the eight hours non-consecutively, if they so wish, and will be expected to post their thoughts on social media after they’ve played, tagging Virgin Media. title: 😰 Google and Microsoft's AI stress test
body_text: One of the hardest parts of life behind bars is going years without your favorite comfort meal. I mean, who would want to go a day without eating Vegemite, the sticky, dark brown tar-like substance made out of leftover brewer’s yeast? Australians, who often enjoy it smeared in a thin layer over white bread, love it so much one man convicted of murder argued it ought to be a human right for him to enjoy some in prison. Unfortunately, the country’s Supreme Court disagreed, upholding one state’s ban of the product in prisons. One of the reasons it’s banned, prison officials argue, is because it could impair sniffer dogs trained to find drugs and alcohol. Alphabet , the parent company of search giant Google, and Microsoft will report earnings today as investors are increasingly seeking data over vibes to reassure them about the continued health of the AI boom. Both companies are expected to report enormous increases in AI-related spending, raising a familiar question: When will all this investment pay off? And here is what the Street is expecting from Microsoft. $46.5 billion in capital expenditures, up 140% from $19.3 billion during the same period last year. $90.6 billion in revenue, up 16.7% from $77.6 billion during the same period last year. $4.71 earnings per share, up 14% from $4.13 last year. And here is what the Street is expecting for Alphabet: $55.2 billion in capital expenditures, up 130% from $23.9 billion during the same period last year. $127.9 billion in revenue, up 25% from $102.3 billion during the same period last year. $3.03 earnings per share, up 5.6% from $2.87 last year. Meta reported results last week and was punished after reporting negative free cash flow and outlining plans to continue spending aggressively on AI. Increasingly, the worry for companies betting big on AI is that they are taking on debt to fund a product that has not quite proven to be lucrative. But not all AI spending is created equal. Meta, importantly, doesn’t have a cloud business (yet). Its AI investments are largely aimed at improving its existing products, particularly its massive advertising business, while developing new AI-powered services. Google and Microsoft, on the other hand, may be spending a ton on AI but they’re also collecting checks from other companies who are also spending a ton on AI. That’s because they, along with Amazon have compute to sell other AI giants. And those deals represent commitments from big AI players to spend figures that can run into the hundreds of billions going forward. A huge amount of power in the AI industry is in cloud giants like Alphabet and Microsoft. These same cloud companies are also investors in, customers of, and suppliers to major AI model developers. Google and Microsoft can justify their enormous spending plans perhaps more than others: They don't necessarily need to build the next killer AI app to make money. They can sell the computing power to whoever does. title: 🐜 $ANT Man
body_text: A campaign is pushing the New York Public Library to return the set of toys that inspired A.A. Milne to write the Winnie-the-Pooh stories to the United Kingdom once and for all. The NYPL owns the actual Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore, Tigger and Kanga, and a cohort of British fans want them returned to commemorate the 100th anniversary. The United Kingdom attempting to get an institution to return an important cultural artifact to its nation of origin? Well, see now I’ve heard everything. Stocks finished up on Monday, led by tech. Yesterday we wrote that the week ahead would be investors’ quarterly check-in on the AI trade. We didn’t know how right we’d be: on Monday, Anthropic filed for its IPO . A couple interesting things pop out that are relevant to companies posting earnings this week, first and foremost the unique arrangement between Anthropic and three cloud service providers (CSPs): Amazon , Alphabet and Microsoft . Sales through the cloud marketplaces of that trio of companies constituted 48% of Anthropic revenue in H1 of this year, up from 11% in 2023. That’s a bit of a double-edge sword; the willingness of the CSPs to shill Claude to their customers has been a significant driver of revenue growth for Anthropic over the period. On the other hand, this means that half the revenue from Anthropic’s customers aren’t actually from Anthropic’ s customers, they’re from Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft’s customers, and you can be certain that those three firms would love nothing more than to swoop in with their own models if the situation were to present itself. But don’t just take our word for it! It’s right there in the prospectus as a risk, “customers may develop their own solutions that compete with our models, platform, and applications.” It’s complicated, and Anthropic isn’t trying to hide that: “Our relationships with our strategic partners — whether with CSPs, who simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors, or with Broadcom , which simultaneously serves as a supplier and lessor — create potential conflicts of interest that are difficult to fully anticipate or mitigate.” Essentially, not only is it complicated, but given how complicated it is we don’t even know how complicated it’s going to end up being. That hasn’t even touched on the unique ownership structure. As a Public Benefit Corporation, Anthropic has not only the founder supervote that’s become common lately, but also a few other tiers of shareholding with various rights and profit participation: Class T shares, for “humanity,” controlled by a long-term benefit trust that appoints four directors who are there to ensure that Anthropic advances the common good. Neat? Class F shares, for the founders, who get the other three board seats. Class E shares, for employees, which have no economic rights but get to break ties. Class A shares. This means you! The economic rights, your slice of the pie. You get a vote, but one that will always be outvoted by the founders anyway. Class N shares, which is Class A stock with no vote, the shares given to Amazon and Google . The next two weeks will be an investor roadshow for the company, and the IPO date is expected to target the week before Thanksgiving under the ticker symbol ANT on Nasdaq. Expectations for the company vary between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion valuation . Compared to the SpaceX prospectus and the kind of language coming out of OpenAI, the document is relatively sober, even if it does contain risk factors like: “Our most capable models have demonstrated, and future models are expected to demonstrate, capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.” “More broadly, the long-term effects of regular AI interaction on mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior are not yet fully understood, and if such long-term harms do materialize in the future, we could face significant liability, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” “Our proprietary model weights, corporate and financial data, and other core intellectual property represent particularly high-value targets for state-sponsored espionage and theft, and security researchers have identified frontier AI companies as priority targets for non-U.S. intelligence services.” Will that make investors skittish?
